title: Volcanoes
standard_text: Volcanoes form where magma reaches the surface; they erupt lava, ash and gases. The Philippines has many active volcanoes (Mayon, Taal, Pinatubo) because it lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire. PHIVOLCS gives alert levels; communities prepare for volcanic hazards. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 6, Quarter 4: Earth and Space)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 4: Earth and Space): parts of a volcano, eruptions, Philippine volcanoes, volcanic hazards and safety, and benefits of volcanoes. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Magma is molten rock underground; lava is magma on the surface.
body_html:
How to think about it

A volcano is an opening in the Earth's crust. Magma from the magma chamber rises through the vent and comes out of the crater as lava, ash and gases. The Philippines lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where tectonic plates meet, so it has many active volcanoes such as Mayon, Taal and Pinatubo.

Volcanic hazards include lava flows, ashfall, pyroclastic flows and lahars. PHIVOLCS watches volcanoes and raises alert levels. Volcanoes also bring benefits: fertile soil, geothermal energy and tourism.

Example

Which volcano is famous for its perfect cone?

In Albay

Answer: Mayon Volcano

Example

What is a lahar?

Ash and water

Answer: a mudflow of volcanic ash and water

Common mistakes

  • Thinking lava is the only danger of a volcano.
  • Thinking an inactive volcano can never erupt.
  • Going back home before PHIVOLCS lowers the alert level.

faq.q: Why are there many volcanoes in the Philippines?
faq.a: It is on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where plates meet.
Underground heat makes steam that turns turbines in geothermal power stations.

items.q: What is a volcano?
c: a mountain made only of ice
an opening in the Earth's crust where magma, gases and ash come out
a deep hole dug by people
items.e: Volcanoes form where molten rock reaches the surface.

items.q: Which layer is described: rigid outer layer of crust and uppermost mantle, broken into plates?
items.e: Layers differ in composition and state.

items.q: Which best describes Earth's asthenosphere?
c: rigid outer layer of crust and uppermost mantle, broken into plates
liquid iron and nickel whose motion makes Earth's magnetic field
thick layer of hot solid rock that moves by slow convection
hot, soft part of the upper mantle that flows slowly
items.e: Match the layer.

items.q: Which evidence supports this claim: “The inner core is solid.”
c: P waves bend and slow down when they enter the outer core.
There is a shadow zone where no direct S waves arrive.
P waves speed up again in the inner core.
Seismic waves slow down in a zone about 100–200 km deep.
items.e: Match the evidence.

items.q: Which agency monitors volcanoes and earthquakes in the Philippines?
items.e: PHIVOLCS gives volcano alert levels.

items.q: What forms where two oceanic plates move apart?
c: a mid-ocean ridge with new crust
items.e: Magma rises to fill the gap.

items.q: Which volcano erupted in 1991 in one of the largest eruptions of the 20th century?
items.e: Ash from Pinatubo cooled the whole Earth slightly for about two years.

items.q: What is an active volcano?
c: a mountain with no magma at all
a volcano that will never erupt again
a volcano that has erupted in historical times or shows signs of activity
items.e: An inactive volcano has not erupted for a very long time.

items.q: Which layer is described: thin, rocky outer layer; thickest under continents?
items.e: Layers differ in composition and state.

items.q: Which volcano lies on an island in a lake in Batangas?
items.e: Taal Volcano is inside Taal Lake.

items.q: What does a higher Volcano Alert Level mean?
c: a greater chance of a dangerous eruption
items.e: Alert levels go from 0 (normal) to 5 (hazardous eruption in progress).

items.q: What is the asthenosphere?
c: a weak, partly molten layer of the upper mantle that flows slowly
items.e: Plates move over it.

items.q: What is magma called when it reaches the surface?
items.e: Magma is molten rock underground; lava is molten rock on the surface.

items.q: How can volcanoes give us energy?
c: their ash is used as gasoline
hot rocks heat underground water to make steam for geothermal power stations
their lava is burned like coal
items.e: The Philippines is one of the top producers of geothermal energy.

items.q: What is a lahar?
c: a mudflow of volcanic ash and water, often after heavy rain
items.e: Lahars from Pinatubo buried towns for years after the eruption.

items.q: Why is volcanic ash dangerous to breathe?
c: it has no oxygen in it
it has tiny sharp particles that can damage the lungs
items.e: Wear a mask and stay indoors during ashfall.

items.q: Which is a benefit of volcanoes?
c: volcanic soil is very fertile for farming
they make the sea fresh water
items.e: Ash breaks down into soil rich in minerals.

items.q: What is a pyroclastic flow?
c: a slow stream of clean water
a fast, very hot flow of gas, ash and rock down a volcano's slope
items.e: Pyroclastic flows are among the most dangerous volcanic hazards.

items.q: Angel studies the Himalayas, where plates push together. What kind of plate boundary is it?
items.e: At a convergent boundary, plates push together.

items.q: Kenneth studies Iceland splitting slowly. What happens to the plates there?
c: The plates slide past each other.
items.e: Iceland splitting slowly is at a divergent boundary.

items.q: What should you do during ashfall?
c: stay indoors, close windows and wear a mask if you go out
wash the ash into the river
items.e: Ash can harm the eyes and lungs.

items.q: What was Pangaea?
c: a supercontinent that existed about 300–200 million years ago
items.e: It broke apart into today's continents.

items.q: Kenneth studies the Alpine Fault in New Zealand. What happens to the plates there?
c: The plates slide past each other.
items.e: The Alpine Fault in New Zealand is at a transform boundary.

items.q: Kristine studies the volcanoes of Japan. What happens to the plates there?
c: The plates slide past each other.
items.e: The volcanoes of Japan is at a convergent boundary.

items.q: Emmanuel studies the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. What happens to the plates there?
c: The plates slide past each other.
items.e: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is at a divergent boundary.

items.q: Diane studies the volcanoes of Japan, where plates push together. What kind of plate boundary is it?
items.e: At a convergent boundary, plates push together.

items.q: Lance studies the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where plates move apart. What kind of plate boundary is it?
items.e: At a divergent boundary, plates move apart.

items.q: Why do many volcanoes and earthquakes happen in the Philippines?
c: it is near the North Pole
it lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire where plates meet
it is far from any plate boundary
items.e: Plate movement causes volcanoes and earthquakes.

items.q: Sheila studies the East African Rift. What happens to the plates there?
c: The plates slide past each other.
items.e: The East African Rift is at a divergent boundary.

items.q: Why couldn't Mesosaurus have swum across the Atlantic?
c: It was a small freshwater reptile that could not cross a salty ocean.
items.e: Its fossils support the idea that the continents were joined.

items.q: About how fast do plates move?
c: a few centimeters per year, about as fast as fingernails grow
items.e: Slow, but it adds up over millions of years.

items.q: Hazel studies the Andes Mountains, where plates push together. What kind of plate boundary is it?
items.e: At a convergent boundary, plates push together.

items.q: Who first proposed continental drift using fossils and continent shapes?
items.e: He proposed it in 1912.

items.q: What is a crater?
c: the bowl-shaped opening at the top of a volcano
the bottom of the magma chamber
items.e: Magma comes out through the vent to the crater.

items.q: What can trigger a landslide?
c: heavy rain, earthquakes or removal of vegetation on steep slopes
items.e: Thredbo (1997) was a landslide disaster.

items.q: Which is a way to reduce the risk of earthquake damage?
c: building codes that require flexible, reinforced structures
items.e: Planning and drills also help.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from wildfires?
c: zoning that keeps homes off the floodplain
clearing brush to make defensible space around homes
water conservation and storing water in reservoirs
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: Why did the 1989 Newcastle earthquake cause so much damage despite a magnitude of only 5.6?
c: it was shallow and close to a city, and some buildings were on soft sediments that amplified shaking
it was far from the city
items.e: Thirteen people died.

items.q: How can a volcanic eruption cool the global climate?
c: ash adds heat to the air
sulfur dioxide forms sulfate aerosols in the stratosphere that reflect sunlight
items.e: Pinatubo (1991) cooled Earth by about 0.5 °C.

items.q: A community plans building codes that make structures flexible and strong. Which hazard is this mainly meant to reduce?
items.e: Match the plan to the hazard.

items.q: A tsunami crosses ocean 2,000 m deep. Its speed is v = √(gd). How long does it take to travel 1,000 km? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
What is pumice?
c: a light volcanic rock full of holes from gas bubbles
items.e: Pumice can even float on water.

items.q: Which signs can warn that a volcano may erupt?
c: small earthquakes, ground swelling and more gas emissions
items.e: Monitoring reduces deaths.

items.q: Which sign may show that a volcano is about to erupt?
c: more earthquakes, swelling of the ground and more gas coming out
items.e: Scientists watch these signs closely.

items.q: A community plans water conservation and storing water in reservoirs. Which hazard is this mainly meant to reduce?
items.e: Match the plan to the hazard.

items.q: About how many times more energy is released by a magnitude 6 earthquake than a magnitude 4 earthquake? (Each step of 1 is about 32 times the energy.)
How many times larger is the ground motion (wave amplitude) of a magnitude 8 earthquake than a magnitude 6 earthquake?
items.e: Each step of 1 is ×10 in amplitude: 10^(8 − 6) = 100 times.

items.q: A community plans clearing brush to make defensible space around homes. Which hazard is this mainly meant to reduce?
items.e: Match the plan to the hazard.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from droughts?
c: monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people
water conservation and storing water in reservoirs
ocean sensors linked to warning sirens
drainage and retaining walls on steep slopes
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: Why do people living near a volcano need an evacuation plan?
c: so that they can leave quickly and safely when an alert is raised
so that they can watch the eruption up close
items.e: Planning saves lives.

items.q: What is a pyroclastic flow?
c: a fast-moving, very hot flow of gas, ash and rock from an eruption
items.e: It is one of the deadliest volcanic hazards.

items.q: A community plans monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people. Which hazard is this mainly meant to reduce?
items.e: Match the plan to the hazard.

items.q: What is the magma chamber?
c: a large pool of molten rock under a volcano
items.e: Magma rises from the chamber through the vent.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms new sea floor?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms rift valleys in East Africa?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms the San Andreas Fault?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a transform boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
the Alpine Fault in New Zealand
the Southern Alps of New Zealand pushing up
items.e: transform (plates slide past each other): the Alpine Fault in New Zealand.

items.q: What forms where an ocean plate sinks under another plate?
c: a deep ocean trench and often volcanoes
items.e: This is called subduction.

items.q: What is liquefaction?
c: waterlogged sand or silt loses strength and behaves like a liquid during shaking
items.e: Buildings can sink or tilt.

items.q: Patricia's town wants to reduce damage from volcanic eruptions. Which technology would help most?
c: storm shutters, stronger roof straps and early warnings from satellites
levees, floodplain maps and raised buildings
buildings with base isolators and flexible steel frames
gas and tilt sensors with evacuation plans
items.e: Mitigation technology matches the hazard.

items.q: Which usually takes longer: a sand dune moving across a desert or a volcanic eruption building a new cone?
c: a sand dune moving across a desert
a volcanic eruption building a new cone
They take exactly the same time.
items.e: Plate-scale changes are the slowest.
